prompt:
I need the front end for Pulsepost. A display configuration service a regional nonprofit blood center uses to run the wall-mounted televisions in its donor lounges, showing current blood supply levels and appeals to donors waiting or walking in.

Who's using it: Renata Oyelaran, 43, donor relations manager at a nonprofit blood center that runs four donation sites and supplies 31 hospitals. She controls what appears on the lounge televisions at all sites. She's comfortable with marketing tools but not with data systems.

What they're doing right now: Monday morning: overnight hospital orders pushed O-negative supply down to 1.4 days, and the center has declared an urgent appeal. Before the 10 am rush, she wants the lounge televisions to put O-negative and platelets front and center. She will change how supply levels are labeled, since staff found 'Critical' alarmed nervous first-time donors, and set the threshold where a type is described as urgent. She also needs to stop showing per-hospital distribution figures, which the medical director says shouldn't be public. The Eastgate site's television sits next to the reception counter, where staff also glance at it, so it should cycle more slowly and keep today's appointment progress in view.

What's in the system at this point: Inventory for 8 red-cell types in days of supply: O− 1.4, O+ 2.6, A− 3.1, A+ 4.8, B− 5.2, B+ 6.0, AB− 7.9, AB+ 9.4. Platelets: 1.1 days (5-day shelf life). Current level labels are Critical (<2), Low (2–3), Stable (3–5), Healthy (>5). The 4 sites are Eastgate, Riverside, Northfield Mall and Mobile Unit 2, each with today's appointments versus goal (Eastgate 58/90, Riverside 41/70, Northfield 33/60, Mobile 2 12/40). The current display content rotates through 5 segments every 12 seconds: supply levels, today's goal, the 7-day collection trend, hospital distribution, and donor milestones. The hospital distribution segment covers 31 hospitals by units shipped this week. The appeal message reads 'O-negative donors: you're needed today.' Last configuration change was 14 Nov by R. Oyelaran.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
